Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]).

$V$ is **finite-dimensional over $F$** when it has a **finite** basis
([[def-linear-basis]], [[def-countable]]): some basis $B$ of $V$ satisfies
$B \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]).

For such a $V$, the **dimension of $V$ over $F$**, written $\dim_F V$, is that
$n$:

$$\dim_F V \;:=\; \text{the unique } n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } V \text{ has a basis } B \text{ with } B \approx n .$$

**This is well defined.** Existence of such an $n$ is the hypothesis, together
with the fact that a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural number
([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 3). Uniqueness is
[[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]]: two bases of $V$ with $n$ and
with $m$ elements force $n = m$. That theorem is therefore a **prerequisite** of
this definition, not a later justification of it, and it is listed in `deps`.

$V$ is **infinite-dimensional over $F$** when it is not finite-dimensional over
$F$, that is, when $V$ has **no** finite basis. No number is attached to such a
space here: the symbol $\dim_F V$ is defined only in the finite-dimensional case,
and the expression $\dim_F V = \infty$ is not used.

**The zero space.** $\varnothing$ is a basis of $\{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-basis]]) and $\varnothing \approx 0$, so $\{0_V\}$ is
finite-dimensional with $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$. Conversely a space of dimension $0$
has a basis $B \approx 0$, that is $B = \varnothing$, and then
$V = \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

For indices $a,b$ in the same finite index set, the **Kronecker delta** is

$$\delta_{ab}:=\begin{cases}1,&a=b,\\0,&a\ne b.\end{cases}$$

Let $i<m$ and $j<n$. The **matrix unit** $E_{ij}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is the
matrix whose $(r,s)$-entry is

$$(E_{ij})_{rs}:=\delta_{ri}\delta_{sj}.$$

Thus $E_{ij}$ has entry $1$ in position $(i,j)$ and entry $0$ everywhere else.
When a dimension is zero, no index of that dimension exists and there are no
matrix units of the corresponding shape.

Let $T:U\to V$ and $S:V\to W$ be linear, with ordered bases $\mathcal B$ of
$U$, $\mathcal C$ of $V$, and $\mathcal D$ of $W$. Then

$$[S\circ T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal D}=[S]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal D}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}.$$

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its
diagonal entries,

$$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

For $n=0$, this is the empty sum, so the unique empty matrix has trace $0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

derivations.claim: If $\dim V=0$, [F1] gives $V=\{0\}$, so its only endomorphism is $D=0$. Assume henceforth $\dim V=m>0$ and choose an ordered basis.

If every entry of the matrix of $D$ were zero, [F2] would make $D$ vanish on every basis vector and hence on every vector. Thus if $D\ne0$ there are indices $i,j<m$ with matrix entry $D_{ij}\ne0$. Define $A(\sum_{k<m}a_kb_k):=a_i b_j$ using the ordered basis chosen in step 1.1. Unique coordinates [F7] make this well-defined; for scalars $\alpha,\beta$ and vectors with coordinate lists $(a_k)$ and $(c_k)$, the coordinate list of their linear combination is $(\alpha a_k+\beta c_k)$, so the formula gives $A(\alpha x+\beta y)=\alpha A(x)+\beta A(y)$. Thus $A$ is an endomorphism. Its matrix sends $b_i$ to $b_j$ and every other basis vector to $0$, so that matrix is $E_{ji}$.

By [F4], the matrix of $D\circ A$ is $[D][A]=[D]E_{ji}$. Row-by-column multiplication [F5] gives $([D]E_{ji})_{kk}=D_{kj}\delta_{ik}$, so every diagonal entry is $0$ except the $(i,i)$ entry, which is $D_{ij}$. By [F6], $\operatorname{tr}(D\circ A)=D_{ij}\ne0$. This contradicts the hypothesis for every $A$. Therefore $D=0$, including the zero-dimensional case from step 1.1.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. If $M$ is free with basis $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $N$ is free with basis $(f_j)_{j\in J}$, then $M\otimes_RN$ is free with basis

$$\bigl(e_i\otimes f_j\bigr)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}.$$

Equivalently, the canonical map $R^{(I\times J)}\to M\otimes_RN$ sending the standard basis vector at $(i,j)$ to $e_i\otimes f_j$ is an isomorphism. This includes an empty basis in either factor.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. The abelian group $M\otimes_RN$ has a unique $R$-module structure for which

$$r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$$

for every $r\in R$, $m\in M$, and $n\in N$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

derivations.claim: For $n=0$, the declared space is $\mathbb C$ with its usual pairing and basis $\{1\}$. For $n>0$, repeated use of [F1] and the associativity identifications in [F2] shows that the lexicographically ordered elementary product vectors form a basis of the tensor space. If one factor basis is empty, the product basis is empty and the tensor space is zero.

Use the coordinates in this product basis to define the pairing by the standard coordinate formula of [F3]. The basis gives unique coordinates by [F5], so this is a well-defined sesquilinear positive-definite pairing. It is linear first and conjugate-linear second by [F3] and [F4].

Write $x_k=\sum_{i_k}x_{k,i_k}e_{k,i_k}$ and $y_k=\sum_{i_k}y_{k,i_k}e_{k,i_k}$ in the supplied bases, using their unique coordinates [F5]. Multilinearity of elementary tensors [F6], applied one factor at a time, gives the coefficient $\prod_k x_{k,i_k}$ of each product-basis vector in $\bigotimes_k x_k$, and similarly $\prod_k y_{k,i_k}$ for $\bigotimes_k y_k$. The standard coordinate formula [F3] therefore gives $\sum_{(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})}\prod_k x_{k,i_k}\overline{y_{k,i_k}}$. Repeated finite distributivity factors this as $\prod_k\sum_{i_k}x_{k,i_k}\overline{y_{k,i_k}}$, which is the displayed product formula. For $n=0$ both expressions are $1$; if a factor has dimension $0$, the product basis is empty and both the tensor pairing and product over factor pairings are $0$.

The product formula depends only on the factor pairings. Any other supplied orthonormal bases therefore give the same pairing on elementary tensors; elementary tensors span by [F1], so sesquilinearity makes the pairings equal everywhere.

The factor permutation in the Definition sends the product basis bijectionally to the product basis in the reordered factors. Unique coordinates [F5] make its linear extension well-defined, and [F7] makes that extension linear; applying the inverse permutation to basis vectors gives the inverse linear map. For the empty list the definition is already the identity.

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $F^{n}$ be the
function space on the von Neumann natural $n = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, with the
pointwise operations ([[def-function-space]], [[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). For $i < n$ define the **standard unit vector**
$e_i \in F^{n}$ by

$$e_i(i) = 1_F, \qquad e_i(j) = 0_F \ \text{ for } j < n \text{ with } j \ne i .$$

Then:

1. **Finite sums in a function space are pointwise.** For every set $X$, every
   $p \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $u : p \to F^{X}$ and every $j \in X$,
   $$\Bigl(\sum_{k<p} u_k\Bigr)(j) \;=\; \sum_{k<p} u_k(j),$$
   the right-hand sum being taken in $(F,+,0_F)$. (Stated here for an arbitrary
   $X$ because the companion page needs it at $X = \mathbb{N}$.)
2. $e : n \to F^{n}$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$ ([[def-linear-basis]]); in
   particular $e$ is injective and its image $e[n] = \{\, e_i : i < n \,\}$ is a
   basis of $F^{n}$ with $e[n] \approx n$ ([[def-equinumerous]]);
3. for every $\lambda : n \to F$ and every $j < n$,
   $\bigl(\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i e_i\bigr)(j) = \lambda_j$; equivalently the
   coordinate list of $x \in F^{n}$ with respect to the ordered basis $e$
   ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) is
   $i \mapsto x(i)$;
4. $F^{n}$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ with $\dim_F F^{n} = n$
   ([[def-dimension]]);
5. at $n = 0$ this reads: $F^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
   so $F^{0}$ is the zero space, the empty list is its ordered basis,
   $\varnothing$ is its basis and $\dim_F F^{0} = 0$.

Every index runs from $0$, so the coordinates of an element of $F^{n}$ are
$x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ and no statement above is restricted to $n \ge 1$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

derivations.claim: For $j,k<d$, the coordinate formula in [F1] gives $\langle e_j,e_k\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{r<d}\delta_{rj}\delta_{rk}$, which equals $1$ when $j=k$ and $0$ when $j\ne k$. Thus the listed vectors are orthonormal.
By [F2] the same vectors form a basis, so they are an orthonormal basis of $Q_d$.
By [F3], the zero-qubit register is the empty tensor product $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$, distinct from the zero-dimensional coordinate space $\mathbb C^0$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $R$ be a unital ring, $M$ a right $R$-module, and $N$ a left $R$-module. Let

$$F:=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$$

be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on the set $M\times N$ ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]], [[thm-universal-property-of-free-modules]]), and write $e_{(m,n)}$ for its standard basis elements. The additive group of $F$ is abelian. Let $H$ be the subgroup generated ([[def-generated-subgroup]]) by all elements

$$e_{(m+m',n)}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m',n)},$$

$$e_{(m,n+n')}-e_{(m,n)}-e_{(m,n')},$$

and

$$e_{(mr,n)}-e_{(m,rn)}$$

as $m,m'$ range over $M$, $n,n'$ over $N$, and $r$ over $R$. Since every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, the quotient group $F/H$ is defined ([[def-quotient-group]]). The **tensor product of $M$ and $N$ over $R$** is

$$M\otimes_RN:=F/H.$$

The coset of $e_{(m,n)}$ is the **elementary tensor** $m\otimes n$. Every tensor is a finite sum of elementary tensors, because every element of $F$ is a finite $\mathbb Z$-linear combination of basis elements and integer coefficients may be absorbed into either additive variable. The defining relations give

$$(m+m')\otimes n=m\otimes n+m'\otimes n,\qquad m\otimes(n+n')=m\otimes n+m\otimes n',$$

and

$$(mr)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn).$$

In particular $0\otimes n=0=m\otimes0$. No $R$-module structure on $M\otimes_RN$ is part of this arbitrary-ring definition; at this stage it is an abelian group.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M,N$ be $R$-modules. The abelian group $M\otimes_RN$ has a unique $R$-module structure for which

$$r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$$

for every $r\in R$, $m\in M$, and $n\in N$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.

The set of **natural numbers** is the **smallest inductive set**
([[def-inductive-set]]),

$$\mathbb{N} = \omega := \bigcap\,\{\, I : I \text{ is inductive} \,\},$$

which exists and is itself inductive by [[lem-omega-smallest-inductive]] (the
Axiom of Infinity, [[def-axiom-of-infinity]], supplies one inductive set to
intersect within, and Separation, [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]], makes the
intersection a set). On $\mathbb{N}$ we take

$$0 := \varnothing, \qquad \sigma(n) := n \cup \{n\},$$

the distinguished element and the successor function. Thus
$0 = \varnothing$, $1 = \{0\}$, $2 = \{0, 1\}$, $3 = \{0, 1, 2\}$, and in general
$n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ is the set of its predecessors.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

For every $n\ge0$, the map
$\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$ of
[[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]] is a bijection. Any permutation of the
$n$ bit positions therefore induces a permutation of the corresponding
computational basis.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

Let $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$ be a finite ordered list of finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces with specified ordered orthonormal bases of
sizes $d_0,\ldots,d_{n-1}$, allowing $d_k=0$. The elementary tensors of the
factor bases, ordered lexicographically, form an orthonormal basis of the
tensor register, and

$$\dim(H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1})=\prod_{k<n}d_k.$$

For the empty list the product is $1$ and the tensor space is $\mathbb C$; if
any $d_k=0$, the tensor space is zero and the product basis is empty.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.

[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with ordered

$$Tz=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}\langle z,e_j\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}f_i, \qquad T=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}T_{ij}|f_i\rangle\langle e_j|.$$

All sums are empty when an index dimension is zero, and the identities include
